newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asian Development Bank threatened by private flows.
newsitem.headline: Asian Development Bank threatened by private flows.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) faces the prospect of becoming irrelevant as private capital flows have usurped the bank's traditional role, ADB president Mitsuo Sato said on Monday.
"Our overarching concern is how we can adapt ourselves to the changing environment ... if we do not do this, we will lose our relevance," Sato told Reuters in an interview.
The ADB, owned by 56 countries, has funded economic development in Asia since it was formed 30 years ago.
Its loans, both on commercial and soft terms, have been crucial in building infrastructure as well as in poverty alleviation projects.
But with the freeing of economies, governments have found enough sources of private funding.

"Lending as such has become less and less significant in view of the increasing flow of private capital across national borders. Increasingly in other words, we will be marginalised, we will be dwarfed ... that is the reason why I am emphasising the need to change ourselves," Sato said.
Figures for Asia were not available but a report by the Institute of International Finance early this year said private capital flows to emerging economies hit record levels in 1996.
The global association of private financial institutions said investment rose 19 percent last year to $231.5 billion and was expected to remain near that level at $231.2 billion this year.
In 1996, the ADB gave loans and made equity investments totalling $5.83 billion, near the previous year's level.
The Manila-based bank is to hold its annual meeting in Fukuoka, Japan, from May 11 to 13 but it is not certain if the bank's future will be discussed at the meeting.
"Whether it will be discussed at the meeting or not, the major concern for us is how we should adapt ourselves to the changing environment," Sato said.
"All shareholders do agree that this is the most important issue affecting the organisation ... but it is not possible to concentrate on this issue at the annual meeting," he said.
Sato said the bank would have to play a catalytic role, making the first few investments in backward regions so that the private sector would be attracted.
ADB funds would also be needed in projects that offered low commercial returns but were important from the environmental and social point of view, he said.
